1:
Three open by remarking how little is known of the man addressed, and all fasten on the same silence. Of Titus, says Barnes, nothing is certainly known but what we find in the epistles, and it is somewhat remarkable that there is no mention of him in the Acts. Clarke finds it strange that of a man of such eminence, to whom a canonical epistle was written, we should know so little: a frequent companion in the journeys, never named in that book. What they gather they agree on: he was a Greek, uncircumcised, brought up in heathenism, and converted by Paul himself, which is what mine own son is taken to mean. Chrysostom argues from the commission instead: Paul would not have given him charge of that whole island, and jurisdiction over so many bishops, without great confidence in him. He dates the letter from its temper: Paul was evidently at liberty, since he says nothing of his trials but dwells continually on grace.

Why the greeting is so formal is asked twice. Ellicott notes that to Timothy the apostle styles himself simply an apostle of Jesus Christ, and thinks the longer title used here because his relations with Titus were less intimate. Calvin gives the harder answer: this extended and laborious commendation of his apostleship shows Paul had in view the whole Church and not Titus alone, for his apostleship was not disputed by Titus. His design was to bring into subjection those who had haughtily rebelled, and he writes not that the epistle may be read in solitude by Titus in his closet, but that it may be openly published. Henry keeps the other end in view, that the highest officers in the church are but servants; Gill, that Paul, once a servant of sin, was by grace made a servant of God.

Ellicott and Robertson correct the same preposition. According to the faith of God’s elect names not a standard by which Paul was chosen but the aim of his apostleship, that through him the chosen of God should believe, the same idiom governing the knowledge, the godliness and the commandment alike. On the God that cannot lie, Robertson notes the adjective occurs nowhere else in the New Testament, and Barnes makes the impossibility the foundation of all our hopes; but Ellicott hears something sharper, suggesting the singular and strong expression was chosen with reference to the peculiar vice of the Cretans, over whose church Titus presided — a glance forward to their own prophet.

Promised before the world began then draws four readings. Barnes takes the purpose to have been formed then, a purpose in the mind of God being equivalent to a promise. Ellicott renders it from eternal ages, the promise resulting from a purpose fixed from eternity. Robertson denies both: it points not to a purpose before time began but to definite promises made in time, long ages ago. Clarke reports that before eternal times is a contradiction in terms, so the true rendering is before the secular times, reckoned by the Jewish jubilees; the foundation of the world means the Jewish economy. On the due times he and Wesley agree: God published the Gospel when it could be published with greatest effect, and it is impossible he should hasten or delay any work of his. His own times, says Wesley, are fittest for his own work — what creature dares ask why no sooner?

The last title divides them flatly. Clarke argues that since the commission was given by Christ alone, the person here called God our Saviour must be Christ only — another proof, he says, that Paul believed Christ to be God. Ellicott holds it must mean God the Father, who fitly possesses the title because through the death of his Son he redeemed us — and notes that the very next verse gives the same epithet to the Son.
5:
Chrysostom takes the leaving-behind as a picture of how that generation worked. The whole life of men in ancient times was one of action and contention; ours is a life of indolence. As if the world had been one house, they divided it among themselves, each taking care of his portion. And he hears no imperiousness in the command: here is a soul free from all envy, not curiously solicitous whether the good was done by himself or another. Where there was danger and difficulty Paul set it in order in his own person; what was attended with honour and praise he committed to his disciple. Henry reads the same facts as diligence, faithfulness in leaving others to cultivate the young plantation, and humility in accepting help from men of smaller gifts.

When this happened must be inferred. Clarke argues that Paul had plainly been in Crete, though it is nowhere else intimated, and could not have evangelised so considerable an island without his historian recording it, so the visit must fall after the Acts closes. Robertson agrees, adding that the verb suggests a more temporary stay than its commoner alternative.

Two words then get pulled apart. Barnes notes that set in order occurs nowhere else in the New Testament and means to make straight upon, and so to put to rights; Robertson calls it a rare double compound, to set straight thoroughly and in addition, a clean job of it. On ordain Barnes is emphatic: the word has since acquired a technical signification which it cannot be shown to have in the New Testament, meaning only to set, place or constitute, without reference to any mode of investment; there is no reason to suppose Titus went through what would now be called an ordination service. Clarke presses the other half: the elders here are the bishops of the next verse, and there are many proofs that bishops and elders were of one order in the apostolic Church, though afterwards they became distinct. Henry keeps Titus above both, inferior to an apostle but set over the fixed pastors, to ordain them where wanting and pass on.

Blameless is at once qualified. Henry will not have it absolute — there is none that liveth and sinneth not, and Christ himself and his apostles were blamed, though not worthy of it — and settles on a man who lies not under an ill character, but has good report even from those without. Ellicott puts it more sharply: the office of presbyter must never be allowed to cover or condone damaged reputations. On the husband of one wife two turn polemical. The church of Rome, says Henry, makes it the husband of no wife, but from the beginning it was not so, marriage being an ordinance from which no calling is a bar; though ministers are not therefore bound to marry. Wesley makes the point in a line — surely the Holy Ghost, by repeating this so often, designed to leave the Romanists without excuse.

Faithful children divides them. Barnes says the word need not mean the children were truly pious, but describes those well-trained and in due subordination. Robertson and Clarke read it as believing, Clarke adding that he who cannot rule his own house cannot rule the church. Ellicott draws a date from it: these elders were to be married men with children already grown, which shows Christianity had stood in Crete a considerable period. On riot he is exact: the word is dissoluteness, implying reckless expenditure, and in men charged with the church funds their homes had to be free of all suspicion of waste. Barnes agrees it would be a good reason now against ordaining a man that he had a dissipated family; Robertson glosses the last word as public disorder, out of doors; Gill keeps to the plainest sense, chargeable with no notorious crime in his outward conversation.
7:
Three settle the identification at once. Gill: this shows a bishop and an elder are the same, and the Syriac renders the word here elder. Ellicott: the bishop must be the presbyter of the verse before, presbyter naming the gravity of the office and bishop rather its duties, and reading bishop in its later ecclesiastical sense here is premature. Robertson puts it in a phrase borrowed from another: elder is the title, oversight is the function. On the steward all agree; Wesley says what the trust is — immortal souls.

The negative qualifications are worked hardest. Barnes finds the first decisive: the word for self-willed occurs nowhere else in the New Testament, and means self-complacent, then arrogant and imperious. The gist of the offence, its very head and front, is the self-complacency, which of necessity makes a man dogmatical, impatient of contradiction and unyielding, and unfit for the office. Clarke describes him from outside: one determined to have his own way in everything, setting his judgment against all others and expecting homage to his understanding — such a governor can do little good and much mischief. On the next he has a choleric man, inflamed on every opposition, without command of his temper; Ellicott says he should never be ready with a hasty word, remembering his Master, who when reviled reviled not again.

The positive list draws out differences. Clarke notes that one manuscript reads lover of the poor for lover of strangers, and turns it into a rebuke: the minister who neglects the poor but visits the rich often knows little of his Master’s work and has little of his spirit. Ellicott keeps the wider sense, hospitality as the epistle to the Hebrews means it, where some entertained angels unawares. Then a real division. Barnes takes a lover of good men and makes it the most essential qualification of all: a minister should love every good man, in whatever denomination or country, whatever his complexion and rank in life. Ellicott thinks it a virtue distinct from hospitality — a lover of good, benevolence generally, the large heart with room for all that is good and noble; Clarke and Robertson read it the same way, of good things in general.

The four that follow Ellicott separates carefully: sober is better rendered self-restrained, the mastery of self that regulates pleasures and passions; the just man performs strictly his duties towards men, the holy man aims at purity before God; and temperate does not repeat the earlier clause about wine but means moderate in all things. Barnes agrees on the last: we now apply the word to abstinence from strong drink, whereas in Scripture it takes in much more, control over all the passions. Clarke, running the four off a line apiece, ends drily that these are qualifications rarely found in spiritual governors.

Holding fast is then given two objects. Barnes reads it as a stand: the elder must hold the word against any who would wrest it away, and as he hath been taught means not as he was taught individually but as the faith was delivered by those the Saviour appointed. Ellicott hears in the faithful saying a formulary common to these letters, echoes of sayings of Christ woven into the earliest liturgies, as comfortable words, as a creed, as a hymn. Robertson glosses the verb as holding oneself face to face with a thing, the gainsayers as the talkers back. On the use of it Barnes divides the labour — exhortation where men know the truth and need encouragement, argument where they are ignorant or opposed — insisting the elder was not to dictate or denounce but to convince by the statement of the truth. Clarke adds the condition: if the doctrine be not sound, vain is the profession of it, and zeal for what is not of God does the souls of men no good, how sincere soever.
10:
Barnes glosses vain talkers as men given to talk rather than to practical religion, and points to Talkative in the Pilgrim’s Progress; Ellicott passes on a description of such men as talkers who must say something, and have broken the peace of many a home; the multitude of teachers with nothing true to say is the curse of the kingdom of God. Clarke has empty boasters of knowledge and privilege, all noise and no work; Robertson renders the second word mind-deceivers. On they of the circumcision all agree that Judaising teachers are meant; Ellicott adds that these were not the rigid Jewish party outside but Paul’s sleepless opponents within the church, and Barnes takes the clause as proof that there were many Jews in Crete.

How the mouths are stopped matters more than that they should be. The verb means to check or curb as with a bridle, says Barnes; Wesley, to put a bit into an unruly horse’s mouth; Robertson, to stop the mouth with bridle, muzzle or gag. Barnes then draws the line the others do not: the apostle gives no civil power to do this, nor calls in the civil arm; the only agency he specifies is argument and exhortation, and the history of the church shows that the ministers of religion can be safely intrusted with no other. Gill and Ellicott supply the model, the silencing of the Sadducees and Pharisees, after which no man durst ask more questions. On the motive Ellicott is blunt: a mean and sordid ambition, base gain; when that is a teacher’s main object his teaching accommodates itself to men’s tastes.

The quoted line is a hexameter of Epimenides of Gnossus. Gill repeats the tale that he turned into a cave at noon and slept fifty-seven years; Clarke says many reckoned him the seventh wise man of Greece, that the Cretans paid him divine honours after death, and that Paul calls him a prophet only because they reputed him one; Ellicott thinks he deserved the title fully; Robertson notes the first half of the line was quoted in a hymn to Zeus. Barnes explains the word: prophet, like the Latin term for a bard, was applied to poets as writing under inspiration, and to any interpreter of the oracles. Wesley says only that all poets were anciently so called.

Chrysostom alone sees a difficulty here, stating it as three questions: who said this, why Paul quoted it, and why he brings forward a testimony that is not correct. The Cretans, he explains, had a tomb of Jupiter inscribed, Here lieth Zan, whom they call Jove, and the poet called them liars for it. But if the poet is true who said they spoke falsely in asserting that Jupiter could die, and the Apostle confirms his testimony, then by the Apostle Jupiter is immortal — a fearful thing. Attend, beloved, with much exactness. His answer is that the Apostle has not said this, but simply applied the testimony to their habit of falsehood; else why did he not add the next line, about the tomb they made? He says only that one had well said, the Cretians are alway liars.

The rest of the line they leave standing. Ellicott observes that the estimate is borne out by profane writers, and that the verb to Cretize was coined as a synonym for to deceive. Robertson calls the evil beasts wicked wild beasts, wonders whether the Minotaur was responsible, and renders the last phrase idle bellies; Wesley glosses it fierce and savage. Henry alone refuses to let the verse rest on Crete: though there may be national differences of character, the heart of man in every age is deceitful and desperately wicked. He also limits the rebuke: Christian meekness is as far from cowardly passing over sin and error as from anger, and the sharpest reproofs must aim at the good of the reproved.
13:
All four take the endorsement at face value, and Gill draws a rule from it. The apostle does not say everything Epimenides wrote was true, only this character of the Cretians, which he cites to a good purpose; whence the writings of the heathen poets may be read with profit if carefully attended to — for what is truth, let it come from whom or by what means it will, ought to be received. Ellicott says Paul had lived long enough among them to bear grave testimony to the words; Robertson, that he endorses it from recent knowledge; Clarke, that what was said six hundred years before was still true, their character having undergone no change.

Sharply gets three glosses. Barnes derives it from a verb meaning to cut off and applies it to manner: Titus was not to be mealy-mouthed, but to call things by their right names and not spare faults. Ellicott takes the same root surgically — as a surgeon’s knife cuts away diseased flesh, so must the words and discipline of Titus — and adds that not only the deceivers are in view but the deceived, the object being that the morally sick be restored to health. Robertson renders it curtly or abruptly and defends it: one must sometimes appear rude for safety, if the house is on fire and life is in danger.

The fables are Jewish. Gill lists some: the feast for the righteous in the Messiah’s days, of Behemoth and Leviathan and wine kept in the grape from the foundation of the world. Ellicott identifies them with what is now in the Talmud, and states the objection precisely: the dread of that school rested on a fear, too often verified, that with the careful observance of ritual the moral law should be lost sight of, holiness coming to consist in keeping a ritual rather than in living justly. Clarke says such men made the word of God of none effect by their traditions, and notes that the verb rendered turn from can mean to despise; Wesley leaves the commandments unattributed, whatever teachers had turned from the truth.

On the famous clause Barnes sets a guard the others do not. The allusion is probably to clean and unclean meats, and the passage should not be read as proving that all things are lawful for a Christian, or whatever he chooses pure; it means there is no sanctity in eating one food and no sin in another. Clarke agrees that to the genuine Christian every meat fit for human nourishment is lawful. Ellicott opens it wider: all things takes in much besides food, all the acts of everyday life which in themselves are neither good nor evil but take their colour from the doer. On the other half Clarke says the defiled are unfaithful to grace offered and received, their minds contaminated with unholy images; Gill defines the pure by exclusion: not such as are so in their own eyes, but those justified by Christ’s righteousness.

The last verse turns on the gap between lips and life, and the two who press it hardest press opposite ways. Clarke turns it against the Jews: none were so full of pretensions to the knowledge of the true God, and they held that to give the law to the Gentiles would be a profanation, whence they became proud and intolerant. He glosses reprobate as adulterate, like bad coin without the sterling stamp. Barnes turns the verse round on the church. Is this character confined to them? Are there none now who profess to know God but in works deny him? Alas, taking the church at large there are many such, and that fact is the grand hindrance to the triumphs of religion. Ellicott adds that these foes present themselves under the guise of friends, and that reprobate means simply useless when any good work had to be done.
